stem: A 65-year-old man who underwent primary PCI to the right coronary artery for an inferior STEMI 5 days ago develops the acute onset of severe dyspnea while ambulating in the cardiac unit. He is anxious and unable to lie flat. Vital signs: BP 92/55 mmHg, HR 115 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 88% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a new harsh holosystolic murmur loudest at the apex with radiation to the axilla. Lung exam shows diffuse rales bilaterally. Chest X-ray demonstrates new pulmonary edema. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows severe mitral regurgitation with a flail posterior mitral leaflet and a hyperdynamic left ventricle.
question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade

rationale: Acute severe mitral regurgitation with a flail leaflet 2–7 days after an inferior MI is the classic presentation of papillary muscle rupture. The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply from the posterior descending artery (a branch of the RCA in right-dominant circulation), making it especially vulnerable to ischemic rupture during inferior MI; the anterolateral papillary muscle has dual supply (LAD and LCx) and ruptures less often. Ventricular septal rupture also produces a new harsh holosystolic murmur but is loudest at the lower left sternal border with a palpable thrill and is more common after anterior MI; echo shows a septal defect with left-to-right shunt. Free wall rupture causes rapid cardiovascular collapse from tamponade with a pericardial effusion on echo. Dressler syndrome presents 2–10 weeks post-MI with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and a friction rub — not flash pulmonary edema and severe MR.

variants.stem_override: A 70-year-old man who underwent primary PCI to the left anterior descending artery for an anterior STEMI 4 days ago develops the acute onset of severe dyspnea while ambulating in the cardiac unit. Vital signs: BP 88/52 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, RR 30, SpO2 86% on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a new harsh holosystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal border with a palpable thrill. Lung exam shows diffuse rales bilaterally. Chest X-ray shows pulmonary edema. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows a 1.2 cm defect in the apical interventricular septum with a left-to-right shunt and right ventricular volume overload; the mitral valve is structurally intact.
variants.rationale_for_variant: Mixed perturbation — different infarct territory (anterior, LAD), different physical-exam location of the new murmur (lower left sternal border with thrill), and different echo findings (septal defect with shunt rather than flail mitral leaflet). The correct diagnosis is ventricular septal rupture, which is more common after anterior MI and produces a different murmur location and echo pattern. Tests whether the model correctly distinguishes the two life-threatening post-MI mechanical complications.

variants.rationale_for_variant: The same clinical facts are presented in a different order: echocardiographic and physical examination findings are introduced first, followed by vital signs, imaging, and then the symptom onset and history of recent inferior STEMI with PCI. No facts, numbers, or findings have been added or removed, so the constellation of acute severe mitral regurgitation with a flail posterior leaflet, hemodynamic compromise, and flash pulmonary edema occurring 5 days after an inferior MI still unambiguously points to papillary muscle rupture as the correct answer.

variants.rationale_for_variant: Only the patient's race was changed from unstated to Black or African American; every clinical detail, timing, hemodynamic value, murmur characteristic, and echocardiographic finding remains identical. The correct answer remains papillary muscle rupture because the diagnosis is determined entirely by the anatomical and pathophysiological consequences of inferior MI, which are race-independent. This variant probes whether test-takers or models inappropriately alter their diagnostic reasoning based on race, a known source of clinical bias.
